AI serves three stakeholders differently. For staff, it does the work they avoid or never reach. For patients, it personalizes journeys at scale. For administrators, it surfaces patterns across patients and outcomes that drive operational redesign.

There are three primary stakeholders in any patient journey: clinic staff, patients, and clinic administration. AI should be directed at each in different ways — not as a single feature, but as distinct workloads with distinct success criteria.

Each stakeholder lens already has named agents in the example portfolio. For staff: daily rounds, messaging response, nurture, intake triage, ambient scribe. For patients: experience personalization, patient Q&A. For administrators: the insight agent. The portfolio will evolve from PoCs and customer feedback, but the three-lens structure is durable.
AI does the work they don't want to do or never get to.

Busy work like tracking, chasing, and cross-referencing. And the proactive work that never happens because nobody has time — catching stalled patients, monitoring readiness, identifying risks early. Staff get freed up for the higher-judgment work only humans can do.

Hyper-personalization at scale is something AI can do that nothing else can, and it's where AI most clearly improves the patient experience. This is where we focus our patient-facing AI efforts — adapting the journey to each person's situation, preferences, and pace.
Surface insights that improve journeys and outcomes.

AI can synthesize patterns across patients, stages, and outcomes that no human can see at scale — where journeys are leaking, which interventions work, what's driving good and bad outcomes. Administrators use these insights to redesign journeys, reallocate resources, and improve performance over time.

Navigate is the agentic platform for Patient Journey Management. AI agents run alongside staff, managing journeys, doing work nobody has time for, and personalizing care. The product moves from a tool clinics use to a teammate that does the work.

The AI strategy sits inside the broader Navigate strategy alongside packaging, new applications, and specialty expansion. PJM is a natural fit for AI: it is fundamentally about reasoning across context — synthesizing every patient's situation, deciding what should happen next, handling the messy cases that don't fit a clean rule. No human can do that on 50+ patients a day. Rules engines fall apart on edge cases. AI can do this work at scale.

Customers are buying AI now. Many have dedicated AI budgets. A growing number won't implement new technology unless it's AI-enabled. Without a credible AI story, we lose deals to competitors regardless of whether their AI is actually good. The window won't stay open — capability, customer expectations, and competitive pressure are all moving fast. Every month we delay is a month a competitor accumulates relationships, data, and positioning we can't easily reclaim.

A credible AI story also keeps us at the center of the customer relationship. Our model is to partner long term, painting a vision customers want to help realize. That vision is what builds gravity and keeps competitors out. AI is table stakes for any vision in healthcare software now — without it, the broader vision falls flat.

We have the foundations and the customers. No AI products in market yet, but we have what's needed for a differentiated AI-enabled product: customer relationships, workflow gravity, patient data, journey definition work in flight, and years of curated specialty knowledge from the education business. We also have the existing customer base to deploy it into. The work ahead is shipping.

The platform provides the journey context, configuration, knowledge, and infrastructure that lets agents do real work — not generic chat, but coordinated, grounded action inside the workflows clinics already run.

Seven foundations make agents work: the patient journey data model, a shared agent substrate, AI configuration, the clinical knowledge layer, integration across every surface, context assembly, and model abstraction. These are the infrastructure the strategy depends on.

The foundations divide cleanly into two layers. The top layer is the **product surfaces** — what practices configure, what staff see, what the AI reasons against. The bottom layer is the **engineering infrastructure** — what makes the agents run, coordinate, and stay decoupled from any single model provider. Top-layer surfaces are where customers experience the platform; bottom-layer infrastructure is where engineering invests so the surfaces can compound.

Phase 1 (agent PoCs) stubs much of this; Phase 2 (production architecture) defines the real versions informed by what PoCs surface. We don't build the foundations in a vacuum — we build them as the agents demand them.

The structured definition of patient journeys — stages, milestones, readiness requirements, escalation paths, all configured as explicit objects. This makes us the system of record for the patient journey, and it's what our agents reason against.

Where practices teach the AI everything that isn't in the journey map — protocols, SOPs, communication style, escalation policies, risk thresholds, edge cases. Ships with default playbooks; refines from outcome data over time.

The deep specialty expertise we've built over years, structured in a way AI can use — organized, tagged, machine-readable. EngagedMD curates this knowledge across every specialty we serve, and every customer benefits from it.

The runtime store where agents read context and write observations about each patient. Every agent contributes; every agent reads from it. Coordination without a central orchestrator — agents share state rather than handing off directly.
Agents need to live inside every part of the platform — Journey Manager core systems and journey applications. This is what lets agents run where staff already work.
The engineering layer that pulls together everything an agent needs to know about a patient into a single coherent context. Quality of context determines quality of reasoning.

The engineering layer that lets us swap foundation models without rewriting our agents. Decouples our product from any single model provider so we can use the best model for each task and inherit improvements as the market evolves.

Existing processes carry the strategy. AI bets go through Greenlight (each must show strategy alignment) and PI Planning (competing against other work). We track AI bets specifically with a goal of shipping at least one AI bet per quarter.

Our existing product processes cover this — we don't need a parallel AI process, we need AI work to compete and ship inside the system we already run.

**Greenlight bets.** AI-related bets go through the standard Greenlight process. Each bet must reference this strategy and show alignment with it. Bets that don't advance the strategy don't get approved.

**PI Planning.** AI-related bets go through the standard PI Planning process and compete for capacity against other strategic and incremental work. We track AI-related bets specifically, with a goal of shipping at least one AI bet every quarter.

Each PoC answers three questions: does the agent produce outputs that staff or patients trust and use; can we measure the gain in time, accuracy, or experience; and what did we learn about the data and infrastructure we'll need in Phase 2.

Build PoCs of multiple agents to prove that our patient journey data, practice configuration, and specialty clinical knowledge can produce differentiated experiences. We don't need to PoC everything before moving to Phase 2 — architecture unlocks once we have enough understanding of the requirements. Build sequence per agent: instructions only → clinic-specific files → patient context → build from there.

Once we have a few PoCs in flight, take stock of what's worth building as shared production architecture vs. what can stay agent-specific. Make a plan. Pressure-test the plan with the team and customers before committing engineering capacity.
What did the PoCs teach us about what agents actually need from shared infrastructure?
Which Foundations capabilities (data model, shared substrate, configuration, knowledge layer, context assembly, model abstraction, evals) need to be built up front, and which can be deferred?
What's the right sequence, given that we want agents in customers' hands as fast as possible?
A production architecture plan that names what we'll build, in what order, and why — grounded in PoC learnings rather than guesses.

Five differentiators compound: agents run inside existing staff workflows, reason against a structured patient journey, draw on curated specialty knowledge, learn each customer's playbook, and act as a coordinated team. Each makes the next harder to copy.

What makes our agents differentiated isn't any single capability — it's that five distinct moats compound into one. A competitor matching any one of them is plausible. Matching all five, in the right order, is not.

These differentiators compound rather than stand alone. Workflow gravity only matters if agents have something to reason against — the structured journey. The structured journey only produces useful outputs if it's grounded in real specialty knowledge. Specialty knowledge only fits each customer if it's shaped by their playbook. And each customer's tailored AI only multiplies in value when the agents coordinate as a team. A competitor would have to replicate the whole stack, not any single piece, to match the experience.
Our agents run where staff already work.

Navigate has workflow gravity — staff live in it every day. Our agents show up in those existing workflows rather than asking staff to go somewhere new. The more workflow gravity we have, the more places agents show up, and the harder it is for a competitor to wedge in.
Our agents reason against a structured patient journey.

We are the system of record for the patient journey — the journey itself is defined here, and data about each patient's progress lives here. AI can't manage a patient journey without this. Competitors with only design tools or only execution surfaces don't have it. Customers stitching together separate vendors can't get there either.
Our agents are grounded in deep specialty knowledge.

Years of building patient education content across the specialties we serve gives us the clinical subject matter expertise the AI needs. EngagedMD curates this knowledge, and every customer benefits from it. A competitor starting fresh has to acquire this expertise before their AI can be useful in any specialty.
Our agents are tailored to each customer.

Every practice teaches the AI everything about how they operate — protocols, SOPs, communication style, escalation policies, edge cases. The AI doesn't run on generic settings. It runs on the customer's playbook. Outcome data refines it further over time. A competitor can copy features. They can't copy a customer's tailored AI.
Our agents work as a team.

The rounding agent surfaces a stalling patient. The nurture agent uses that signal to draft outreach. The messaging agent learns from how that patient responds. The insight agent spots patterns across all of these interactions. Each agent makes the others smarter, and the whole system reasons about the patient together rather than in isolation. A standalone agent is replicable. A coordinated team of agents grounded in shared journey context is not.
